summaries.example: Imagine a rule-checking machine for math. The symbol □A means “there is a correct proof of A in our chosen rulebook.” The special GL rule says that if the rulebook can prove “if A has a proof, then A is true,” then the rulebook can prove A. This sounds strange, but Löb’s theorem shows that the rule really works only in the expected, limited way.
summaries.summary: Provability logic is a branch of modal logic about mathematical proofs. It treats “is provable in a particular formal theory” as a special operator, written □. The entry explains the history of this idea, including questions inspired by Gödel and Henkin and Löb’s surprising answer. Its main system is GL, which has ordinary logic rules plus a special rule about provability. The entry also describes fixed points, which allow formulas to imitate self-reference in a controlled way. GL has mathematical models, including possible-worlds models, and it is both sound and complete for an important part of Peano Arithmetic: GL proves exactly the modal patterns that Peano Arithmetic proves under suitable translations. The entry also introduces stronger and broader versions of provability logic and explains why formal provability is more precise than vague ideas about what people can know or prove.
key_ideas: Provability logic studies what a mathematical rulebook can say about its own proofs.
The symbol □ is used for “is provable in a chosen theory,” such as Peano Arithmetic.
The main system, called GL, grew from work connected with Gödel’s and Löb’s theorems.
A fixed point lets a formula describe itself without needing a messy self-reference.
GL matches an important part of what Peano Arithmetic can prove about its own provability.
summaries.why_it_matters: Provability logic helps mathematicians study the limits of formal rulebooks. It turns difficult questions about proofs and self-reference into a precise logical subject. This connects to major results about incompleteness and consistency, while also showing that “true” and “provable” are not always the same thing.

important_terms.definition: A carefully defined list of rules and starting statements used to make mathematical proofs.
A statement saying that a particular statement has a proof inside a formal theory.
A kind of logic that studies ideas such as “must be true” or, here, “can be proved.”
A sentence or idea that refers to itself, such as “This sentence has a proof.”

questions_to_think_about: Why might “being true” and “having a proof” be different?
What could go wrong when a sentence talks about itself?
Why would mathematicians want rules for talking about proofs?
Can a rulebook prove that it never makes a mistake?

summaries.example: Let □A mean “Peano Arithmetic proves A.” The central GL principle is □(□A → A) → □A. It does not simply say that every provable statement is true inside the theory. Instead, Löb’s theorem says that if Peano Arithmetic proves □A → A, then it already proves A. Thus a formal theory cannot generally establish its own reliability for A unless A is already obtainable in the theory.
summaries.summary: Provability logic studies a restricted language in which the modal operator □ means provability in a fixed arithmetical theory. Its central propositional system, GL or Gödel–Löb logic, extends basic modal logic with the axiom □(□A → A) → □A. This axiom reflects Löb’s theorem: a theory can prove the claim that its proof of A would guarantee A only when the theory already proves A. The fixed point theorem gives a systematic way to replace certain forms of self-reference with a formula that is equivalent to its own provability-based description, and it establishes uniqueness up to GL-equivalence. Semantically, GL corresponds to transitive, conversely well-founded frames and is complete even for finite irreflexive trees. However, its usual semantics is not compact, so strong completeness for arbitrary infinite assumption sets fails. The major arithmetic result is Solovay’s theorem: under every appropriate realization of □ as arithmetic provability, a modal formula is provable in Peano Arithmetic exactly when it is a theorem of GL. The entry then surveys extensions involving interpretability, propositional quantifiers, multiple provability predicates, and predicate logic.
key_ideas: GL extends basic modal logic with the Gödel–Löb axiom and standard rules such as Modus Ponens and necessitation.
Löb’s theorem explains why the GL axiom is appropriate for formalized provability rather than ordinary necessity or knowledge.
The fixed point theorem shows that controlled self-reference can be replaced by a uniquely determined formula without the self-referential variable.
GL is sound and complete for suitable transitive, conversely well-founded Kripke frames.
Solovay’s arithmetical completeness theorem connects the decidable modal system GL with the much richer theory of Peano Arithmetic.
The entry distinguishes formal provability from informal or absolute ideas of mathematical knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject provides a rigorous bridge between modal logic, metamathematics, and the foundations of arithmetic. It explains how formal systems can represent claims about their own proofs without treating provability as the same as truth or knowledge. Because GL is decidable while arithmetic is much less manageable, its modal semantics offers a useful way to investigate a precise fragment of arithmetic self-reference.

important_terms.definition: A modal logic in which □ is interpreted as provability in a fixed formal arithmetic theory.
The propositional provability logic known as Gödel–Löb logic; its distinctive axiom is □(□A → A) → □A.
A formal arithmetic theory used in the entry as a principal example of a sufficiently strong theory.
A metamathematical result stating that if a theory proves “if A is provable, then A,” it proves A itself.
A formula B satisfying B ↔ A(B), where a variable in A occurs only within provability operators; GL proves that such B is unique up to equivalence.
The property that every GL theorem remains provable after □ is translated as the theory’s arithmetized provability predicate.
Solovay’s result that GL proves exactly the modal formulas whose every arithmetic realization is provable in Peano Arithmetic.
A semantic condition on a class of frames: every finite satisfiable part of a set of formulas is satisfiable, a condition that GL fails in its usual semantics.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the principle □A → A behave differently for provability than for knowledge or necessity?
How does the fixed point theorem clarify the role of self-reference?
Why can GL be complete for finite formulas while failing strong completeness for infinite sets of assumptions?
What does Solovay’s theorem reveal about the relationship between modal semantics and arithmetic?
Why might adding quantifiers or several provability operators change the behavior of the logic?

summaries.example: Suppose a school’s math rulebook uses □A for “the rulebook has a proof of A.” Someone asks whether the rulebook can prove: “If the rulebook can prove A, then A is correct.” Löb’s theorem gives a surprising answer: if the rulebook really can prove that statement, then it can prove A itself. So the statement is not a powerful shortcut for proving new facts. It works only when A was already provable.
summaries.summary: Provability logic is a modal logic built to study what formal arithmetical theories can express about their own provability. In its basic language, ordinary propositional connectives are joined by □, read as “is provable in a fixed theory,” often Peano Arithmetic. The main system is GL, or Gödel–Löb logic. Its characteristic axiom reflects Löb’s theorem, which says that if a theory proves that the provability of A would make A true, then the theory already proves A. This distinguishes formal provability from familiar modal ideas such as necessity and knowledge. A central fixed point theorem shows that when a variable appears only under □, a formula can be replaced by a self-contained equivalent formula, and that the result is unique in GL’s sense. The entry also presents Kripke-style semantics: GL corresponds to transitive frames with no endlessly ascending chains, and it is complete for finite tree-like frames. Yet strong completeness fails because an infinite set of assumptions may have every finite part satisfiable while the whole set is not. Solovay’s arithmetical completeness theorem establishes the deepest connection: GL proves exactly those modal formulas that every suitable arithmetic realization makes provable in Peano Arithmetic. Later sections describe extensions for interpretability, quantified propositions, stronger provability notions, and predicate logic.
key_ideas: Provability logic uses □ to talk about proofs inside one chosen theory, not about every kind of certainty.
GL combines ordinary propositional reasoning with a special axiom derived from the behavior of formal provability.
Gödel’s incompleteness results helped motivate questions about sentences that discuss their own provability or unprovability.
The fixed point theorem shows that some self-referential patterns can be represented without leaving the ordinary modal language.
Possible-worlds semantics gives GL a mathematical model theory, but infinite collections of assumptions reveal a failure of strong completeness.
Solovay’s theorem says that GL captures exactly the propositional modal information about provability that Peano Arithmetic can establish.
summaries.why_it_matters: Formal mathematics often needs to reason about proofs, consistency, and the limits of its own rules. Provability logic supplies a compact language for doing this. It also clarifies why results about Gödel incompleteness should not be casually transferred from formal provability to broad claims about human knowledge or mathematical truth. The theory is therefore important both technically and philosophically.

important_terms.definition: A formal system for discussing possibility, necessity, or another special kind of operator.
The claim that a statement can be derived by the rules of a particular formal theory.
A formal theory of arithmetic used in the entry to represent natural numbers, addition, multiplication, and proof coding.
The modal system GL, named for Gödel and Löb, designed to describe formal provability.
A theorem saying that if a theory proves “provability of A implies A,” then the theory proves A.
A formula that reproduces a provability-based description of itself; the fixed point theorem says such formulas can be constructed and are unique in the relevant sense.
A translation that assigns arithmetic sentences to propositional atoms and replaces □ with an arithmetic provability predicate.
A proof-theoretic or semantic result saying that all and only the appropriate valid formulas are captured by a logical system.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a formal proof different from a statement being true in the natural numbers?
How does Löb’s theorem limit what a theory can say about its own reliability?
Why is GL not simply the same as a logic of knowledge?
What does a possible-worlds model contribute to the study of provability?
Why might researchers want versions of the logic with several provability operators?
